---
title: "Research"
description: "Geospatial approaches to climate, cities, landscapes, and environmental decision-making."
---

The Van Berkel Lab develops and applies geospatial methods to understand how communities and landscapes change under environmental and societal pressure. A recurring goal is to move beyond analysis alone: we design methods, visualizations, and decision-support systems that make complex spatial information usable in real-world choices.

## Climate adaptation, migration & urban futures
We study how climate change may alter where people live, how cities grow, and what new pressures migration may place on housing, infrastructure, environmental quality, and equity. Our work combines land-change modeling, demographic scenarios, climate information, and stakeholder engagement.

## Geospatial artificial intelligence
Our research uses computer vision, vision-language models, remote sensing, and spatial machine learning to extract actionable information from large image and spatial datasets. Current applications include residential property conditions and blight in Detroit, wildlife and conservation communication, and species-interaction inference.

## Participatory GIS & decision support
We develop participatory mapping systems that enable residents and practitioners to identify risks, priorities, preferences, and tradeoffs. PIVOT and related tools link these inputs with spatial models so that local knowledge is not merely collected but becomes part of scenario analysis and planning.

## Flood resilience & climate knowledge
Through GLISA and CHIRRP/PUMP-COR, we examine how climate, hydrologic, and community knowledge can be brought together to support flood planning. This includes work in Benton Harbor, Milwaukee, Detroit, and other Great Lakes communities.

## Human–environment relationships
We use social media, surveys, landscape visualization, and spatial analysis to understand how people perceive and value nature. This work spans cultural ecosystem services, conservation, recreation, urban forests, and the ways digital media shapes environmental engagement.

## Methods
Our work commonly draws on **GIS · spatial statistics · R · Python · remote sensing · machine learning · large language models · agent-based and cellular-automata modeling · social media analytics · street-level imagery · participatory GIS · interactive visualization · Shiny/Leaflet · qualitative and mixed methods**.
